title: Finite-coset averaging on continuous homogeneous cochains
statement:
Let $E$ be a topological field [def-weil-field]. For a topological group $J$ and a topological $E$-vector space $V$ with jointly continuous $E$-linear $J$-action, write $B^n(J,V)$ for the abstract $E$-vector space of jointly continuous functions $F:J^{n+1}\to V$ with $F(ax_0,\ldots,ax_n)=aF(x_0,\ldots,x_n)$. Its differential is $(\delta F)(x_0,\ldots,x_{n+1})=\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}(-1)^jF(x_0,\ldots,\widehat{x_j},\ldots,x_{n+1})$, and it is extended by zero in negative degrees. Let $G$ be a compact topological group and $H\subseteq G$ an open subgroup with the subspace topology. There is a finite transversal $S\subset G$ for the right cosets $H\backslash G$, containing $1$ as representative of $H$, with $|S|=[G:H]$. For any such $S$, the uniquely determined map $r:G\to H$ given by $x=r(x)s$ for the unique $s\in S$ representing $Hx$, is continuous, satisfies $r(hx)=h r(x)$ for $h\in H$, and restricts to the identity on $H$.
For every topological $E$-vector space $V$ with jointly continuous linear $G$-action, the formulas
$$(T_{V,n}f)(x_0,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{s\in S}s^{-1}f(r(sx_0),\ldots,r(sx_n))$$
define an $E$-linear cochain map $T_V:B^\bullet(H,V)\to B^\bullet(G,V)$. Put $a_s(x)=s^{-1}r(sx)$, using $H\subseteq G$. These maps $G\to G$ are continuous. For $a\in G$, let $\pi_a(s)=u$ be the unique representative with $Hsa=Hu$. Then $\pi_a$ is a permutation of $S$ and $a_s(ax)=a a_{\pi_a(s)}(x)$. If $R_V$ is restriction of homogeneous cochains to $H$, then
$$(T_{V,n}R_{V,n}F)(x_0,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{s\in S}F(a_s(x_0),\ldots,a_s(x_n)).$$
For the same $S$ and $r$, simultaneously for all $V,W$ and every continuous $G$-equivariant $E$-linear map $b:V\to W$, postcomposition $b_*$ satisfies $b_*T_V=T_W b_*$. No normality of $H$, completeness or local compactness of $V$, or discreteness of its topology is assumed.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic expansion below the coefficient comparison: compactness, finite right-coset retraction, homogeneous averaging, equivariance, differential compatibility, composite with restriction and coefficient naturality. Agent-written auxiliary lemma from old transfer proof steps 2–4 and 9, not stated verbatim in the blueprint.

proof.text: The spaces $B^n(J,V)$ and their differentials are well defined directly from the stated formulas. Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication preserve continuity and equivariance. Each deletion of one coordinate is continuous and commutes with simultaneous left multiplication, so $\delta$ preserves these properties and is $E$-linear. In $\delta^2F$, for each pair of original positions $i<j$, deleting $i$ then the position $j-1$, or deleting $j$ then $i$, gives the same value with coefficients $(-1)^{i+j-1}$ and $(-1)^{i+j}$. They cancel. Thus these are cochain complexes, also after extension by zero in negative degrees.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 1; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text: The right cosets $Hx$ cover $G$ and are open: right translation by $x$ is a homeomorphism, with inverse right translation by $x^{-1}$. Compactness, namely the finite-subcover property, gives a finite subcover by such cosets. Two right cosets that intersect are equal, since $h_1x=h_2y$ implies $x=h_1^{-1}h_2y$. Discard repetitions and choose one representative of each coset, using $1$ for $H$. This gives $S$. Its cardinality is the number of right cosets, equal to $[G:H]$ (inversion bijects right and left cosets).

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 2; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text: Fix any such $S$. If $x\in Hs$, there is a unique $h\in H$ with $x=hs$, namely $h=xs^{-1}$; define $r(x)=h$. On the open set $Hs$, this is the continuous map $x\mapsto xs^{-1}$ into the subspace $H$. Explicitly, for an open subset $U\subseteq H$, its inverse image under $r$ is $\bigcup_{s\in S}Us$, which is open in $G$: $U$ is open in $G$ because $H$ is open, and right translations preserve opens. Hence $r$ is continuous. For $h\in H$, $hx$ lies in the same right coset as $x$, and $hx=(hr(x))s$, so uniqueness gives $r(hx)=hr(x)$. On $H$ the representative is $1$, giving $r(x)=x$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 3; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text: For $a\in G$, right multiplication gives a bijection $Hx\mapsto Hxa$ of the set of right cosets, with inverse right multiplication by $a^{-1}$. It therefore permutes their representatives: write $u=\pi_a(s)$ and $h_s=sa u^{-1}\in H$, so $sa=h_su$. Then $r(sax)=h_sr(ux)$, and consequently $a_s(ax)=s^{-1}h_sr(ux)=a u^{-1}r(ux)=a a_u(x)$. Also $x\mapsto a_s(x)=s^{-1}r(sx)$ is continuous, by continuity of translation, $r$, and the inclusion $H\subseteq G$. More explicitly, $\pi_{a^{-1}}(\pi_a(s))=s$ because $(Hsa)a^{-1}=Hs$, and the reverse composite is the identity by the same equality with $a^{-1}$; thus the reindexing used below has a specified inverse.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 4; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text: For $f\in B^n(H,V)$, the tuple map $(x_0,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto(r(sx_0),\ldots,r(sx_n))$ is continuous, since each coordinate is continuous. Composing with $f$ and then with the continuous linear action of the fixed element $s^{-1}$ gives a continuous function into $V$. Summing these functions over finite $S$ is continuous by repeated use of continuous addition in $V$. Each summand depends $E$-linearly on $f$, so the displayed formula for $T_{V,n}$ is $E$-linear.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 5; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text:
Using $u=\pi_a(s)$ and $h_s$ from step 4, $H$-equivariance of $f$ gives
$$s^{-1}f(r(sax_0),\ldots,r(sax_n))=s^{-1}h_s f(r(ux_0),\ldots,r(ux_n))=a u^{-1}f(r(ux_0),\ldots,r(ux_n)).$$
Sum this identity and reindex by the permutation $s\mapsto u$. Since the action of $a$ is linear, the result is $(T_{V,n}f)(ax_0,\ldots,ax_n)=a(T_{V,n}f)(x_0,\ldots,x_n)$. Together with step 5, this proves that $T_{V,n}$ takes values in $B^n(G,V)$. In formulas, $\sum_{s\in S}a\pi_a(s)^{-1}f(r(\pi_a(s)x_0),\ldots,r(\pi_a(s)x_n))=a\sum_{u\in S}u^{-1}f(r(ux_0),\ldots,r(ux_n))$, using the inverse permutation from step 4.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 6; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text:
At $(x_0,\ldots,x_{n+1})$, expand $\delta T_{V,n}f$ as
$$\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}\sum_{s\in S}(-1)^j s^{-1}f(r(sx_0),\ldots,\widehat{r(sx_j)},\ldots,r(sx_{n+1})).$$
Interchange the two finite sums. The $E$-linear action of $s^{-1}$ commutes with signs and addition, so the inner sum over $j$ is $s^{-1}(\delta f)(r(sx_0),\ldots,r(sx_{n+1}))$. Thus $\delta T_{V,n}=T_{V,n+1}\delta$. In negative degrees take $T$ to be the unique zero map; the remaining cochain-map identities then have both sides zero.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 7; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text:
Restriction $R_{V,n}$ takes $B^n(G,V)$ to $B^n(H,V)$: the inclusion $H^{n+1}\subseteq G^{n+1}$ is continuous, and $G$-equivariance implies $H$-equivariance. Restriction is linear and commutes term by term with deletion, hence with $\delta$. For $F\in B^n(G,V)$, use its $G$-equivariance with $s^{-1}$ in each summand to obtain
$$s^{-1}(R_{V,n}F)(r(sx_0),\ldots,r(sx_n))=F(s^{-1}r(sx_0),\ldots,s^{-1}r(sx_n)).$$
Summing gives exactly the asserted $T_VR_V$ formula.

source.place: Paragraph (3), arithmetic auxiliary expansion: 8; explicit argument by Q138, not a verbatim blueprint proof.

proof.text:
For a continuous $G$-equivariant $E$-linear $b:V\to W$, composition $b_*$ preserves continuity and equivariance for both $G$ and $H$, and commutes with $\delta$ because it preserves finite signed sums. With $S,r$ fixed independently of the coefficients,
$$b\bigl(\sum_{s\in S}s^{-1}f(r(sx_0),\ldots,r(sx_n))\bigr)=\sum_{s\in S}s^{-1}b\bigl(f(r(sx_0),\ldots,r(sx_n))\bigr).$$
Here linearity moves $b$ through the sum and equivariance moves it through each $s^{-1}$. This is $b_*T_V=T_Wb_*$ simultaneously for every $V,W,b$. All sums are finite; no division by the index or limiting operation occurs.
